results.title: Model Interpretability Techniques That Actually Work: Expert Analysis
results.content: Model interpretability techniques are essential for researchers who need to understand how their machine learning models arrive at specific predictions or decisions. Though several important model-agnostic interpretability methods exist, none are perfect—yet they remain valuable tools for interpreting even highly complex machine learning models. We'll analyze the limitations of methods like Partial Dependence Plots, ICE plots, surrogate models, and SHAP values, while providing guidance on how to choose and validate the right interpretability approach for your specific needs. Interpreting complex machine learning models presents significant challenges for data scientists. When features are dependent, perturbation-based techniques like Permutation Feature Importance (PFI), Partial Dependence Plots (PDP), LIME, and Shapley values can produce misleading results. This leads to evaluating the model in areas of the feature space with little or no observed data, where model uncertainty is exceptionally high. For interpretations to be valid, both the original model and any secondary analysis must accurately capture the data-generating process. If a deep learning model fits the data well but a post hoc analysis with LIME doesn't sufficiently capture the original model's behavior, the resulting interpretations will be inaccurate. By understanding these limitations, we can approach model interpretability techniques with appropriate caution and select methods that match our specific analytical needs. ## Limitations of Popular Model Interpretability Techniques. PDPs operate at an aggregated level, averaging all data points to create a single curve that shows the marginal effect of a feature on model predictions. For example, in a model predicting heart attack risk using a person's weight from yesterday and today (highly correlated features), the importance splits between both features since either provides similar predictive value. LIME (Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations) encounters a significant challenge: explanation instability. This becomes problematic with interpretability techniques that might oversimplify complex models. Some common pitfalls include over-relying on visualizations without statistical grounding, assuming feature independence in correlated datasets, and ignoring model-specific behavior when using model-agnostic tools. Surrogate models can lose fidelity to the original complex model, suffer from local instability in their explanations, and introduce sampling bias when generating perturbed instances. results.content: Automated Assessment of Fidelity and Interpretability: An Evaluation Framework for Large Language Models’ Explanations (Student Abstract) Mu-Tien Kuo1, 2, Chih-Chung Hsueh1, 2, Richard Tzong-Han Tsai2, 3 1Chingshin Academy, Taiwan 2Research Center for Humanities and Social Sciences, Academia Sinica 3Dept. For interpretability, we use language models instead of human evaluators, addressing concerns about subjectivity and scalability in evaluations. In conclusion, our framework streamlines the evaluation of explanations from LLMs, pro-moting the development of safer models. Introduction As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain traction, it is of increasing paramount to evaluate their explanations’ quality. A well-crafted explanation hinges on two elements: fidelity, which refers to a truthful representation of the model’s inner-workings, and interpretability, which pertains to the ease with which humans can comprehend it (Gilpin et al. Our work focuses on evaluating free-text rationales, which are model-generated natural language explanations and the predominant format of LLMs’ explanations. Although eval-uation methods for rationales have considerable develop-ment, there are sizeable limitations on applying prior meth-ods to SOTA LLMs. Traditional fidelity evaluations often assumed full access to the model, enabling commonly used methods such as extracting rationale salience maps via gra-dients (Atanasova et al. The traditional practice of comparing machine-generated explanations to human-written ones is inherently flawed as this measures only narrow aspects of text (Wiegreffe, Marasovi´ c, and Smith 2021) and show minimal correlation Copyright © 2024, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (). To assess utility, we use the forward simulatability metric, evaluating informativeness based on how well an auxiliary model can forecast a model’s decision based on its expla-nation, and brevity by observing the performance drop of the auxiliary model when various amounts of explanation information are removed. Lastly, as difficult language (such as complex vocabulary or nonstan-dard sentence structure) hinders interpretability, Cognitive Salience (CS) evaluates the readability and complexity of the language in the explanation. Conclusion In this study, we introduced a task-agnostic framework for evaluating the quality of free-text rationales in terms of both fidelity and interpretability. We apply our frame-work in evaluating GPT-3.5’s explanations, finding fidelity decrements when prompted to produce explanations that are faithful, caused by a misinterpretation of faithfulness. results.content: Local surrogate models, at their core, are like your personal interpreters — they help you translate the decisions of your complex neural networks into something understandable and actionable. A local surrogate model is a simple, interpretable model (like a linear regression or decision tree) that approximates your complex neural network’s behavior around a specific prediction. from lime.lime_tabular import LimeTabularExplainer# Initialize the LIME explainerexplainer = LimeTabularExplainer( training_data=X_train_scaled, # Use the scaled training data feature_names=X.columns, # Provide feature names for better interpretability class_names=['Negative', 'Positive'], # Adjust according to your problem mode='classification' # Set the mode: 'classification' or 'regression')# Explain a single instanceinstance_idx = 10 # Replace with the index of the test instance you want to explainexplanation = explainer.explain_instance(X_test_scaled[instance_idx], model.predict)# Display the explanation (useful for Jupyter Notebooks)explanation.show_in_notebook(). Throughout this guide, I’ve shared the steps I take to make complex neural networks more interpretable using local surrogate models like LIME and SHAP.
